title: Grammar-constrained decoding
subtitle: A grammar compiled from the tool registry constrains the decoder so that names outside the catalog cannot be produced.

stats.label: per token cheaper than unconstrained decoding
extra round trips per query in the old no-repeat loop
what the industrial stack's workaround cost

lede: Capabilities model answers an agent's discovery call with a ranked list of tool pointers. A small model can produce a plausible tool name that does not exist, and an agent that calls a fictional tool fails slowly and confusingly. I decided validity belonged in decoding. I also decided the constraint should make decoding cheaper. The grammar compiles from the tool registry, through the same frozen contract the evaluation scores against, into a trie over the model's own token ids. One compiled source feeds both the evaluation constraint and the serving constraint, so what was measured is what is served, and a registry change regenerates the grammar along with the training data.
quote: I treat a constraint as information the hardware can use, and I put guarantees where they can be enforced, with their exact scope stated.
evidence: Constrained decoding for LLMs: a grammar compiled from the tool registry into a trie over token ids, so a tool name outside the catalog has no edge to take and cannot be produced.
CUDA kernel development: masking in the sampling kernel with no-repeat counts on trie edges and the trie in constant memory, making decoding 172 microseconds per token cheaper than unconstrained.
Inference serving architecture: no-repeat moved from a server-side loop costing 5.58 extra round trips per query to one on-device decrement per completed tool.
author: Corey James
